preacher.name: D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones
preacher.tradition: Reformed evangelical: began his ministry at a Forward Movement (Calvinistic Methodist) church in Wales, then served Westminster Chapel, London, a church founded as Congregational that left the Congregational Union and joined the FIEC during his pastorate
preacher.bio: David Martyn Lloyd-Jones was born in Cardiff on 20 December 1899 and grew up in Llangeitho, Ceredigion. He trained in medicine at St Bartholomew's Hospital, London, and from 1921 was assistant to the royal physician Sir Thomas Horder. In 1927 he left medicine to become minister of the Bethlehem Forward Movement church, Sandfields, Aberavon (Port Talbot). In 1939 he became associate pastor of Westminster Chapel, London, alongside G. Campbell Morgan. He was sole pastor from Morgan's retirement in 1943 until he retired in 1968 because of illness, which Wikipedia describes as a major operation. He preached for the last time in June 1980 at Barcombe Baptist Chapel and died at his home in Ealing on 1 March 1981.
preacher.corpus_note: The MLJ Trust says its free online archive holds over 1,600 sermons from his Westminster Chapel ministry (1939–1968). It also says his sermons were not recorded until 1953, so earlier series such as the Sermon on the Mount survive only in print. Many series were edited into books after he retired, including a 14-volume Romans, whose first volume appeared in 1970 according to the Trust. The set is now published by Banner of Truth.

sermons.title: Studies in the Sermon on the Mount
sermons.published_in: Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, 2 vols. (London: Inter-Varsity Fellowship, 1959–1960)
sermons.summary: This is an exposition of Christ's Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), published as sixty studies that go through the passage in order. Lloyd-Jones explains each section and applies it to Christian life and conduct. Because it covers the whole sermon, it includes Christ's teaching on not taking revenge and on loving one's enemies (Matthew 5:38–48).
sermons.context: According to the MLJ Trust, Lloyd-Jones preached through Matthew 5–7 at Westminster Chapel in 1950–51. His sermons were not recorded until 1953, so no audio of this series survives. Transcripts of the sermons became his first published book (1959–60). Citing Iain Murray, the Trust says publishers had lost interest in printed sermons at the time, and that Lloyd-Jones remarked the book brought him more letters from the United States than anything else he wrote.

sermons.title: Spiritual Depression: Its Causes and Cure
sermons.published_in: Spiritual Depression: Its Causes and Cure (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1965), 21 sermons
sermons.summary: The series asks why Christians lose their joy and assurance and takes the causes one at a time. The opening sermon discusses temperament, physical condition and the devil. Later sermons deal with a particular past sin, vain regrets, fear of the future, and relying on feelings. The opening sermon on Psalm 42:5 traces spiritual depression finally to unbelief. It urges believers to talk to themselves from what God has revealed about himself and his promises, rather than being ruled by their moods.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust dates the series to 1954 at Westminster Chapel. It quotes Lloyd-Jones's own account from Iain Murray's biography: while he was dressing one morning, Psalm 42:5 suddenly came to him with outlines for several sermons, and he felt he had to preach them before moving on to Ephesians. The Trust dates the first Ephesians sermon to 3 October 1954. Eerdmans published twenty-one of the sermons in 1965, and the book has been in print ever since.

sermons.title: Ephesians sermon series
sermons.published_in: Edited into a multi-volume exposition published from 1972 (e.g. God's Way of Reconciliation on Ephesians 2; Christian Unity on Ephesians 4:1–16; Life in the Spirit in Marriage, Home & Work on Ephesians 5:18–6:9; The Christian Warfare on Ephesians 6:10–13)
sermons.summary: This is a verse-by-verse exposition of Paul's letter to the Ephesians in over 230 sermons. It starts with the spiritual blessings, election and redemption of chapter 1. It then covers salvation by grace and the reconciliation of Jew and Gentile in chapter 2, and the unity and growth of the church in chapter 4. It ends with Christian conduct in marriage, family and work, the armour of God passage, and prayer in chapter 6.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust says the series of 232 sermons was preached on Sunday mornings at Westminster Chapel from 1954 to 1962. Its first recorded sermon is dated 3 October 1954, and 'Praying for All the Saints' on Ephesians 6:18–20 is dated 8 July 1962. The Trust records that in 1959 he interrupted the Ephesians series to preach on revival. It also quotes Iain Murray: after retiring, Lloyd-Jones chose to publish his Romans sermons first, followed by those on Ephesians.

sermons.title: Romans sermon series
sermons.published_in: Romans, 14 vols. (first volume 1970; now Edinburgh: Banner of Truth Trust)
sermons.summary: This is a consecutive exposition of Paul's letter to the Romans in 366 sermons, from Paul's opening self-description in 1:1 to Romans 14:17. Lloyd-Jones regarded Romans as first in importance among the New Testament letters. He works in turn through sin, atonement and justification by faith (3:20–4:25), assurance (chapter 5), the new man (chapter 6), the law's functions and limits (7:1–8:4), sonship and the perseverance of the saints (chapter 8), and the practical teaching of chapters 12–14.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust says the sermons were preached on Friday evenings at Westminster Chapel from October 1955 to March 1968. They ran from October to May each year, with breaks at Christmas and Easter. The Trust calls this his longest expository series and says he saw it as his most important work. The first recorded sermon is dated 7 October 1955, and the Trust dates its sermon on Romans 14:17 to 1 March 1968, the year he retired. The Trust quotes Iain Murray that Lloyd-Jones chose these sermons to be published first, and it dates the first volume to 1970.

sermons.title: Revival
sermons.summary: These sermons argue that the church's powerlessness cannot be cured by apologetics, modern evangelistic techniques, new Bible translations or advertising, but only by the power of God sought in prayer. Lloyd-Jones uses texts such as the disciples' failed exorcism in Mark 9 and Isaac re-digging his father's blocked wells in Genesis 26. He defines revival as a work of the Holy Spirit among God's people and unbelievers. He says false teaching about the Spirit must be cleared away, and calls the whole church to prayer.
sermons.context: According to the MLJ Trust, the sermons were preached in 1959 to mark the 100th anniversary of what it calls the Welsh Revival of 1859. The Trust says he interrupted his Ephesians series to preach them because he considered the subject urgent. Crossway published them as a book in 1987.

sermons.title: The Cross: God's Way of Salvation
sermons.published_in: The Cross: God's Way of Salvation, ed. Christopher Catherwood (Westchester, Ill.: Crossway Books, 1986)
sermons.summary: This is a run of sermons on a single verse, Paul's statement that he will boast only in the cross of Christ. Lloyd-Jones argues that salvation comes only through Christ dying in the place of sinners, received by faith, not through human merit. He says the cross shows up the emptiness of a world run by the lust of the flesh and the pride of life, and that it defeated the devil. He also argues that pride is the root of divisions of race, nation and class, and that the cross removes it by showing everyone to be equally sinful and in need of the same salvation.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust dates ten recorded Galatians 6:14 sermons to Sundays from 20 October to 22 December 1963 (nos. 5583–5592). One of them, 'The Middle Wall of Partition' (24 November 1963), deals specifically with human division and enmity. Nine of the sermons, described as preached at Westminster Chapel in autumn 1963, were edited by Christopher Catherwood and published by Crossway in 1986.

sermons.title: Preaching and Preachers
sermons.occasion: Lectures to students and faculty (16 lectures plus two question-and-answer sessions)
sermons.published_in: Preaching and Preachers (1971; US edition Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1971)
sermons.summary: These lectures argue that preaching is the church's most urgent need and primary task. Lloyd-Jones attributes its decline to lost belief in the Bible's authority, to treating the sermon as a literary essay, and to reliance on ceremony, entertainment and counselling in its place. Later lectures cover the call to preach, the congregation, the preparation of the preacher and the sermon, the form and shape of the sermon, illustration, eloquence and humour, what to avoid, and altar calls and music in relation to true conversion. He ends by arguing that power in preaching depends on the Holy Spirit's anointing ('unction'), which preachers must seek.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust says he gave the series to students and faculty at Westminster Theological Seminary in spring 1969, shortly after retiring from Westminster Chapel. His retirement freed him to accept the seminary's longstanding invitation, which his weekly preaching load had previously prevented. The Trust notes that R. C. Sproul, then a young man, attended and later recalled hearing the lectures.

sermons.title: True Love
sermons.summary: On Paul's command that husbands love their wives as Christ loved the church, Lloyd-Jones separates three Greek words for love: eros (physical desire), phileo (natural affection and fondness), and agape (self-giving love). He argues that a husband's love must be agape, modelled on Christ's devotion to a church that was far from perfect. He insists that a husband's authority must be governed by love and not become tyranny. He also rejects the teaching that the physical side of marriage is inferior to celibacy.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust dates this sermon (no. 4165) to Sunday 14 February 1960. Its number falls within the Trust's numbering for his Sunday-morning Ephesians series at Westminster Chapel, which reached Paul's teaching on marriage at this point.

sermons.title: Love Your Neighbour
sermons.summary: Lloyd-Jones argues that modern people misunderstand love of neighbour. They reduce it to sentiment, and they put it before love for God, reversing the order Jesus taught. He separates the Greek words for love and argues that people made self-centred by sin cannot truly love their neighbour as themselves. Only those who are born again and indwelt by the Holy Spirit can show agape love, so sound doctrine and new birth are the foundation of neighbour-love, not obstacles to it.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust dates this sermon (no. 3344) to Friday 3 March 1967, in the Friday-evening Romans series at Westminster Chapel. It is the second of three consecutive Friday sermons on Romans 13:8–10. It comes between 'Love Fulfills the Law' (24 February 1967) and 'Scriptural Love' (10 March 1967).

sermons.title: Because He First Loved Us
sermons.summary: On the sinful woman who anointed Jesus' feet in the house of Simon the Pharisee, Lloyd-Jones contrasts two responses to Jesus. Simon kept a cold, formal distance and did not show him the usual courtesies. The woman, aware of her sin, washed his feet with her tears and anointed them. He argues that the measure of a person's love for Christ is their sense of how much they have been forgiven. He says true religion centres on the person of Christ rather than on knowledge about him, and that God's law drives sinners to see their need of the only one who can forgive them.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust dates this sermon (no. 5378) to Sunday 19 September 1954 and does not place it in a series. That is two weeks before his Ephesians series began. The page does not name the venue.

sermons.title: Overcoming Evil
sermons.summary: On Paul's instruction to feed a hungry enemy and to overcome evil with good, Lloyd-Jones argues that Christians must do more than refrain from revenge: they must actively do good to those who wrong them. He urges hearers to see an opponent as a lost person in need of redemption, and to recognise the evil and spiritual forces at work behind him, rather than treating him as a personal rival. He describes three kinds of victory: over evil in oneself, over the adversary, whom kindness may shame into repentance, and over evil itself.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust dates this sermon (no. 3331) to Friday 11 November 1966, in the Friday-evening Romans series at Westminster Chapel. It followed 'God's Wrath, Not Man's' on Romans 12:19–20 (4 November 1966). In that sermon, according to the Trust's summary, he argued that vengeance belongs to God and that the ban on personal revenge applies to individuals, not to the state.

sermons.title: He is Our Peace
sermons.summary: On Paul's statement that Christ broke down the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile, Lloyd-Jones argues that Christ ended that enmity through his death on the cross. He did this by abolishing the ceremonial law that kept the two apart and making them one body. Lloyd-Jones insists that peace between people depends first on peace with God. He says the world's continuing conflicts come from lacking that reconciliation, which cannot be understood without seeing humanity's separation from God.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust dates this sermon (no. 4054) to Sunday 19 February 1956, in the Sunday-morning Ephesians series at Westminster Chapel. The next Sunday's sermon, 'Christ's Way of Making Peace' (26 February 1956, Ephesians 2:15), applied the passage, warning that divisions in the church by race, age or nationality contradict Christ's work.

sermons.title: The Fellowship of Believers
sermons.summary: From the account of the first converts in Jerusalem, Lloyd-Jones argues that real conversion leads naturally into the fellowship of the church. He rejects the idea of a Christian who has no need of it. He roots this fellowship in a shared new life, outlook, experience and Saviour, which makes believers one family across differences of nationality, temperament and social class. He contrasts the early church's eager daily gathering with modern reluctance to attend.
sermons.context: The MLJ Trust dates this sermon (no. 2007) to Sunday 21 February 1965. It belongs to his Sunday-evening series on Acts at Westminster Chapel (1965–1968), which the Trust calls his largest collection of evangelistic sermons, preached on the assumption that not everyone in the congregation was converted.

sermons.title: Address to the National Assembly of Evangelicals
sermons.occasion: National Assembly of Evangelicals, organised by the Evangelical Alliance; chaired by John Stott
sermons.summary: Lloyd-Jones called on evangelicals to withdraw from 'mixed' denominations in which they were united with people who deny or oppose what he called the essential matters of salvation. The question at issue was whether evangelicals should stay in such denominations or leave them.
sermons.context: John Stott chaired the meeting. He was not scheduled to speak that evening, but used his position as chairman to disagree publicly, saying Lloyd-Jones's view went against history and the Bible. Wikipedia reports that the clash was widely covered in the Christian press and caused considerable controversy. The Evangelical Alliance's own history says the public disagreement led to the Alliance losing some members.

sources.label: Evangelical Alliance – Our history (1966 Stott–Lloyd-Jones disagreement)
